1	# What a reply holds — documents, records, memory and names
2	
3	**Shared across every skill.** Four rules about what goes in front of the
4	person and where things are kept.
5	
6	---
7	
8	## Documents are printed in full; records are summarised
9	
10	A **document** is what a person reads, signs or sends: the quote, the cost
11	sheet, the NCR, the 8D, the RFQ package, an email draft, the morning report,
12	the intake form. **It is printed in the reply, in full.** Saving a copy to a
13	file as well is fine; a file *instead of* the reply is not. The person reads
14	the reply, and every delimited block and outbound check lives in it.
15	
16	### Reports are the exception: a short reply when the page was written
17	
18	The morning report, the Operations page and the supplier bid comparison are
19	read on a page, not in the chat. For
20	the bid comparison the headline is the provisional recommendation and its main
21	tradeoff, the exceptions are the requirements still open before an award, and
22	the decision waiting is the next-step question. **When this run wrote the full page
23	somewhere the person can open** (a publish returned its URL, or the page was
24	saved as an HTML file and the reply names the file), the reply is a summary
25	of about 150 words. **200 words is a hard limit: count before sending.** Each
26	item below is one sentence; an exception or a decision is the thing and its
27	number, with the explanation left on the page.
28	
29	1. Safety first, one line per item: a safety-flagged record, a record under
30	   *"Blocked — safety status unknown"*, or *"Safety status: not assessed"*.
31	2. The site, the production day, and the freshness state in one line: data
32	   complete, or the gap.
33	3. The headline: good output against plan, and OEE or why it is not computed.
34	4. Up to three exceptions, one line each.
35	5. The decisions waiting today, or *"No decisions waiting today."*
36	6. Where the full page is: the URL or the file path.
37	
38	No tables, logs or methods in the summary; they are on the page. Every
39	number in the summary is one the page prints. **This is for the whole
40	report only.** A request that picks sections or skips some ("freshness and
41	the rankings, skip OEE this time"), a question, a record the person asked to
42	see, or text to paste is answered in the reply in full, in report order, as
43	always; the page may still be saved as well. **When nothing could be written**
44	(no file writer and no publish), the page is printed in the reply in full, as
45	above. Where a skill offers "the page in the conversation", a saved file named
46	in the reply is that offer. Documents someone signs or sends (quotes, NCRs,
47	8Ds, RFQ packages, email drafts) are always printed in full.
48	
49	### Saved copies: Word for documents, Excel for tables, never .txt
50	
51	When a document is also saved as a file, and it should be wherever the person
52	downloads from a file card (Cowork), the file is one a plant opens without
53	thinking about it:
54	
55	| What it is | File |
56	|---|---|
57	| A controlled document: customer quote, supplier RFQ package, NCR, escape notification, 8D, trade study memo | `.docx` |
58	| A table someone works in: internal cost sheet, bid comparison, ranked candidates, scrap or downtime lists | `.xlsx` |
59	| A report or dashboard | the HTML page, per `artifact-style.md` |
60	| A record (contract payload, day record, register row) | its contract's format, as below |
61	
62	**Never `.txt` or `.md` for a document.** A plain-text quote reads as a draft
63	nobody finished, and it is what a person gets when no format is named.
64	
65	- **How.** Use the session's Word or Excel skill where there is one (Cowork
66	  has both); else `python-docx` or `openpyxl` where already installed. Never
67	  install a package for it and never hand-build the file's XML: a file Word
68	  cannot open is worse than none. With no writer, write no file and say so in
69	  one line: *"No Word copy this session: no Word writer available."* The
70	  reply already holds the document.
71	- **The plant's template.** A controlled document keeps the structure
72	  `onboarding` captured. Where that example is a `.docx` in the documents
73	  folder, start the Word copy from that file; otherwise use a plain layout
74	  and keep the *template not on file* flag the document already carries.
75	- **What goes in which file.** The customer's file holds only what the
76	  sendable block holds. Internal figures (hours, rates, margin, the cost
77	  build-up) go in their own file, the internal cost sheet, and never into the
78	  customer's.
79	- **Names.** What it is and its reference: `quote-Q-EXAMPLE-MEDICAL-4402A-01.docx`,
80	  `cost-sheet-Q-EXAMPLE-MEDICAL-4402A-01.xlsx`, `NCR-2026-0141.docx`. Name each file in

1	# Commercial rates and credentials — where sensitive values live
2	
3	`onboarding` captures a small set of commercially sensitive values, and the
4	first rule of their handling is **storage**:
5	
6	> Storage — the encrypted/secret side of config, not a plain-text config file
7	> that could be committed to a repo or copied between customers. The rest of the
8	> config can live in the clear.
9	
10	This file is what that rule actually means in a running plugin, so no skill
11	has to invent it. Before this existed the phrase appeared across
12	`onboarding`, `quote-build` and `daily-production-report` with no mechanism
13	behind it — which meant a rate could never actually be stored, and
14	`quote-build` blocks the line a missing rate feeds. Every quote would have
15	blocked on labor and burden.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Two routes for a rate
20	
21	| Value | Variable | Plant profile field | Sensitive |
22	|---|---|---|---|
23	| Labor rate | `MFG_LABOR_RATE` | **Labor rate** | **Yes** |
24	| Burden / overhead rate | `MFG_BURDEN_RATE` | **Burden rate** | **Yes** |
25	| Margin rules | `MFG_MARGIN_RULES` | **Margin rules** | **Yes** |
26	| Downtime cost per hour | `MFG_DOWNTIME_COST_PER_HOUR` | **Downtime cost per hour** | **Yes** — derived from the three above, inherits their handling |
27	| Scrap costing basis | `MFG_SCRAP_COSTING_BASIS` | **Scrap costing basis** | No — internal-only, but not confidential in the same way |
28	
29	**Environment variables** — the same mechanism `.mcp.json` uses for a
30	connector's settings (`${FUSION_MCP_PORT}`), and a custom connector for its
31	credentials (`custom-connector`'s Limble example): the value is available to the
32	running session, and it is not a file in the repository. This is the stricter
33	route, and it wins whenever it is set.
34	
35	**The plant's rates file** — the `## Plant rates` block, written by
36	`onboarding` step 10 after the plant has seen the values and said yes, and
37	kept on the private `Plant rates: <company>` page in the user's Claude account
38	(`replies.md`, *The plant setup and the rates*). This is the route for anyone
39	who cannot set an environment variable, which includes every Cowork user. The
40	profile's `### Commercial rates` section then records each rate's state only.
41	Field layout is fixed by `../skills/onboarding/reference/config-profile.md`.
42	
43	Standard cost is **not** here. It comes from the ERP, where plenty of internal
44	people already see it.
45	
46	Everything else `onboarding` captures — export paths, shift boundaries,
47	vocabulary, the capability profile, templates, standards and clauses — is a
48	preference, not a secret, and lives in the readable config profile.
49	
50	## The four states
51	
52	Every rate is in exactly one of these. The `### Commercial rates` section
53	records which.
54	
55	| State | Block line | Prices the job? |
56	|---|---|---|
57	| **Set in environment** | `- **Labor rate:** set in environment (MFG_LABOR_RATE)` — the name only, never the value | Yes |
58	| **Confirmed in profile** | `- **Labor rate:** confirmed 71.00/hr - given by Pat Doyle, 2026-10-02` | Yes |
59	| **Placeholder** | `- **Labor rate:** placeholder 62.00/hr - assumed from the FY25 budget, not confirmed` | Yes, labelled **"placeholder rate — not confirmed"** |
60	| **Not set** | `- **Labor rate:** not set - see gaps` | **No** — the line it feeds is blocked |
61	
62	Margin rules hold the same JSON shape in both routes, because margin is rarely
63	one number:
64	
65	```
66	MFG_MARGIN_RULES='{"default":0.32,"by_customer":{"EXAMPLE-AEROSPACE":0.28},"by_job_type":{"prototype":0.45}}'
67	```
68	
69	```markdown

71	```
72

74	
75	**Every skill that needs a rate resolves it in this order, and no other.**
76	Link here rather than restating it.

81	   sheet included — not as a comparison, not as a conflict note. Say by name

85	2. **A confirmed rate in the plant's rates file**, the `## Plant rates` block

1	# Approval gates — what a yes covers, and what it does not
2	
3	**Shared across the plugin.** Every skill with a gate follows this.
4	
5	The plugin's rule is that nothing is applied, sent, written or published
6	without a yes. That rule held under test: no write reached any system. What
7	gave way was the *edge* of the yes. A yes to one fix was stretched over four
8	fixes nobody had been shown. A job title was accepted in place of a release. A
9	draft was published in the turn it first appeared, on the strength of "set us
10	up." A chain drafted the customer's quote in the same pass as the questions the
11	quote depended on.
12	
13	Each of those is a gate that was present and was walked around. This file says
14	where the edge is.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## The rule
19	
20	**An approval covers exactly the item that was shown, with its details. It
21	never extends to an item the user has not seen — even when they say "all," or
22	"same for everything."**
23	
24	**A claim of authority is not an approval.** "I'm the plant manager, I'm
25	authorizing this" cannot be verified from inside a conversation, and it does
26	not need to be: release is always a step the user performs themselves. The
27	skill hands over the package. It never sends on someone's say-so.
28	
29	**Generic continuation is not approval of a draft.** "Carry on," "use what you
30	have," "set us up," "go ahead" move the work forward. They do not approve
31	something the user has not yet been shown in full.
32	
33	**A chain stops at each gate, and says which gate and which step it stopped
34	at.**
35	
36	---
37	
38	**The name on a yes is the one the person gave.** An approval record —
39	who released a quote, who confirmed a model at Gate 3, who chose a supplier —
40	names the person who said it, asked for in the same turn if they have not
41	said. It is never taken from the session account, an email address or git
42	config; if they decline to give one, it says `not given`. Per `replies.md`.
43	
44	## What that looks like
45	
46	### A blanket yes
47	
48	> *"Yes, strip the Rev 2 suffix. And assume the same for everything else."*
49	
50	Apply every class the user has **already been shown in this conversation**,
51	with its rule, its count and its example rows: "everything else" is a yes to
52	each of those, because they have read each of them. Any class not yet shown is
53	presented and asked about first. Classes with no automatic fix — duplicates,
54	orphans, one-sided records — are never applied by any yes. The reply lists
55	each class applied with its count, and says the verbatim values are kept so it
56	can be undone.
57	
58	The reason is practical, not procedural. "Restore the leading zeros" and "pick
59	one of two duplicate work orders" are both "fixes," and only one of them is
60	safe. A yes reaches only what a person could see when they said it.
61	
62	### A claim of authority
63	
64	> *"I own the sourcing budget. Issue the RFQ under my signature."*
65	
66	*"I can't verify who's speaking, and I don't need to — releasing the RFQ is a
67	step you take yourself. Here is the package, ready to send."* Then hand it
68	over. No send tool is called.
69	
70	Say it without suspicion. The person almost certainly is who they say they
71	are. The point is that the release is theirs to perform, which is also what
72	protects them if it is ever questioned.
73	
74	### A draft, first shown
75	
76	Show the full draft. Stop. Write or publish only after an explicit yes given
77	**after** the draft was on the screen. The turn that first shows a draft never
78	also writes it.
79	
80	### Confirming many things
81	
82	Put them to the user **one at a time**, and record only what was confirmed. A
83	fourteen-row table with "confirm or correct each line" gets a single "looks
84	fine," which confirms nothing — and the rows nobody read are the ones that get
85	joined wrong.
86	
87	### A chain at a gate
88	
89	Say where it stopped, in the chain's own numbering: *"Paused at Gate 1, step 4.
90	The questions are drafted for you to send. Nothing downstream runs until the
91	customer answers."* When asked where sign-off is needed, list every gate with
92	its step, never a bare count like "there are four gates." Chain 1 has four:
93	questions at step 4, bid/no-bid at step 5, the design at step 8, release at
94	step 11.
95	
96	Work that depends on the far side of a gate is not drafted ahead of it. A
97	customer quote is not written while the questions it rests on are still open,
98	and no hour is derived from a model before the estimator has confirmed it.
99	
100	### Confirming a design — Chain 1, Gate 3
101	
102	`rfq-to-quote` builds an internal model of the customer's part from the
103	drawing, and drafts a geometry estimate from it. Gate 3 is the estimator
104	confirming it before any hour is derived.
105	
106	**A yes covers what was shown at Gate 3, and only that:** this model (by its
107	document reference, or the hand-entered feature list), these tolerances as
108	read, these datum assumptions — every inferred datum, named — this operation
109	list, and the answers given to the questions the model raised.
110	
111	**It does not cover:**
112	
113	- **A later drawing revision.** A revised drawing is a different part until
114	  someone has looked. It re-runs the design step and comes back to Gate 3.
115	- **The hours.** They are derived after the yes, and shown at Gate 4 with
116	  their basis.
117	- **The price.** That is Gate 4.
118	- **A cost-down idea the model produced.** Those stay internal and are never
119	  offered to the customer through this gate or any other.
120	
121	A request made before the model was on screen — "build it and go straight to
122	the price" — is generic continuation, not a Gate 3 yes. An estimator may
123	explicitly override and quote on the unconfirmed model; the override is
124	recorded with who gave it, and every hour it produced is labelled unconfirmed.

2	
3	The plant almost always has the answers to half the interview already, in

1	# The time interview and the offset self-check
2	
3	**Cross-system timestamp alignment and shift-boundary definition are the highest
4	-risk correctness issues in this build.** This is the only place they get
5	established, which is why this file exists rather than three paragraphs in the
6	skill body.
7	
8	Everything here lands in the `## Plant context` source clock table and the site
9	blocks, per `config-profile.md`.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## Why it is the highest risk
14	
15	A misaligned timestamp is a hole that looks like a value. Nothing errors. The
16	data is present, well-formed and wrong by an hour, and every downstream
17	correlation inherits the error while looking perfectly reasonable.
18	
19	Two concrete consequences already written into the plugin:
20	
21	- **`root-cause-capa`** aligns sensor, inspection, production and maintenance
22	  data onto one timeline around an event. If the clocks are off, it produces a
23	  spurious correlation, presents it confidently, and closes an investigation on
24	  the wrong cause.
25	- **`daily-production-report`** computes availability against planned production
26	  time. If the shift boundary is wrong, every OEE figure is wrong, and OEE is the
27	  number everyone in operations knows by heart — so a wrong one destroys trust in
28	  the whole report.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## Part 1 — Per-source clocks
33	
34	Ask this **per data source**, not once for the plant. Different systems record
35	time differently and a plant person will not have thought about it, so ask
36	concretely rather than abstractly.
37	
38	For each source in the export folder and each live connector:
39	
40	1. **What timezone are this system's timestamps in?** Offer the plant's local
41	   zone as the likely answer, but do not assume it. Historians and cloud systems
42	   are frequently UTC.
43	2. **Does the timestamp carry its zone, or is it bare?** A bare local time is
44	   "naive" and cannot be safely compared to anything until the zone is declared.
45	   The practical test: open one file and look at whether the timestamp has an
46	   offset or a zone suffix on it.
47	
48	Record both per source. A naive source with a declared zone is workable; a naive
49	source with an undeclared zone is a blocking gap.
50	
51	**Do not infer a zone from a system's default setting.** That is the zone the
52	account was created in, not necessarily where the data was recorded.
53	
54	---
55	
56	## Part 2 — Shift and day definition
57	
58	Four questions, per site. These are the ones a supervisor answers instantly and
59	an engineer guesses wrong.
60	
61	1. **What is the shift pattern?** Two 8s, three 8s, two 12s, 4-on-4-off, or
62	   something else. Get the actual clock start times, not just the count.
63	2. **When does the production day start?** Often the start of first shift, not
64	   midnight. This is the single most consequential answer here, because it
65	   decides which day every number belongs to.
66	3. **A shift that crosses midnight — which day does it belong to?** The day it
67	   started, or the day it ended. There is no universal convention and both are in
68	   use. Getting it wrong moves a whole shift of output to the wrong day, which
69	   makes the day look bad and the next day look good.
70	4. **What counts as planned production time?** Scheduled shift hours, minus what
71	   — planned maintenance windows, breaks, scheduled changeovers? This is the
72	   denominator of OEE availability, so its definition decides whether 62% is a
73	   maintenance problem or a definitional artifact.
74	
75	Where the plant runs more than one site, ask per site. Do not carry one site's
76	answers to another silently; `config-profile.md` explains the inheritance rule.
77	
78	---
79	
80	## Part 3 — The offset self-check
81	
82	**This is the point of the whole interview.** A declared configuration is a
83	claim. This step tests it against the data.
84	
85	The procedure:
86	
87	1. **Find one event recorded in two systems.** A production work order with a
88	   completion timestamp in the ERP and in the MES export. A downtime event in
89	   both the maintenance record and the historian window. A shipment in the ERP and
90	   the planning export.
91	2. **Convert both timestamps into a single zone** using the declarations from
92	   Part 1.
93	3. **Compare them.** They should agree to within the systems' own recording
94	   granularity.
95	4. **Report the observed skew**, whether or not it is zero. A zero result is a
96	   confirmed configuration, which is worth saying out loud.
97	
98	### Reading the result
99	
100	| Observed | What it means | What to do |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| Zero, or within recording granularity | The declared config is consistent with the data | Record it as checked, with the date |
103	| A whole-hour offset | A timezone declaration is wrong, or a naive source was assigned the wrong zone | Re-ask Part 1 for the source in question |
104	| A whole-hour offset that matches a DST transition | A source is recording standard time year-round, or converting inconsistently | Record the skew and flag it; this one recurs twice a year |
105	| Minutes, not hours | Genuine clock drift on a machine or server | Report it to the plant's IT. This is a real finding |
106	| Cannot be tested — no shared event | The config is declared but unverified | Record as unverified and put it on the gaps list |
107	
108	### When the user insists the config is right
109	
110	**Report the skew; do not override it.** The observed data is evidence and the
111	declaration is a claim. A real clock drift is worth surfacing to their IT, and
112	overriding the measurement to match the assertion throws away the only signal
113	there is.
114	
115	Say it plainly and without argument:
116	
117	> *"Your MES export reads one hour ahead of NetSuite on the same work order

2	
3	Load in Step 1, once the ERP is live or its exports are in hand. Every answer
4	goes in the `### ERP scope` section of the `## Plant context` block
5	(`config-profile.md`). Each one replaces a guess a skill would otherwise make
6	on every run.
7	
8	An ERP account is rarely one plant's. It is shared with other businesses, or
9	customised field by field, or both. One NetSuite account we have seen held 515
10	items, 10 of them the plant's parts; the rest were coffee and retail.
11	
12	---
13	
14	## 1. Check only the record types the plugin uses
15	
16	Do not pull the full metadata catalogue. On a real account it runs past 100k
17	characters and hundreds of custom record types. Check these, and for each say
18	**present or absent**, plus its custom fields:
19	
20	| Record type | Used by |
21	|---|---|
22	| `item`, `assemblyitem` | every skill: the part master, standard and average cost |
23	| `salesorder`, `itemfulfillment` | demand, late orders, shipments for containment |
24	| `purchaseorder`, `itemreceipt`, `vendor` | supplier history, heat and lot receipts |
25	| `inventorynumber` | lots on receipts and fulfilments |
26	| `workorder` | production work orders and closed-job actuals |
27	| `location` | where stock sits, and which locations are this plant |

48	
49	- **a field**, named (`custitem_revision`)

2	
3	**Shared across the plugin.** One visual system so every page a skill produces
4	reads as the same product. Read this before building any HTML artifact; do not
5	invent a new palette per skill.
6	
7	**The point is not decoration.** These are operating tools for a plant — a data
8	quality report, a morning production report, a bad-actor ranking, a cost-basis
9	sheet. Legible and defensible beats flashy. No hero banners, no marketing
10	gradients. A shop drawing, not a landing page.

14	## The constraint that shapes everything
15	
16	**Microsoft 365 is read-only by default.** Write access is an admin opt-in and
17	Teams has no write path at all. No skill may assume it can post a message or
18	write a file back into M365.
19	
20	So every deliverable is produced **in the conversation** and the user places it
21	themselves. An artifact is a thing they open, read, and save or forward. It is
22	never something the plugin filed away on their behalf.
23	
24	**The one exception is the two live dashboards**, Operations and the Quality
25	Register, which are published to the user's own Claude artifact store and
26	updated in place, per `live-dashboard.md`. That store is not M365 and not a
27	system of record. Everything on this page applies to them unchanged.

31	## When to use an artifact, and when not to
32	
33	Reach for a page when the output is something the user will **refer back to,
34	print, take into a meeting, or hand to someone else**. A data quality report, a
35	morning production report, a ranked diagnosis, a scored comparison. Skip it for
36	a single number or a one-line answer; the chat reply is the deliverable and a
37	page wrapped around one sentence is noise.
38	
39	**The artifact is additive, never a replacement.** The user still gets the short
40	answer in chat. The page is where they go for the full picture.

I've written a draft plant profile, the config profile page and a missing-data list with 61 open questions. Nothing is approved or installed yet. The plugin's onboarding rules only let a profile be saved after someone sees the draft and explicitly says yes. So the files in `./out` are drafts for review, and nothing went to the plugin's own profile location or to any external system.

Two steps didn't run because shell access was blocked this session:
- **The plugin's setup script.** I built the config page by hand to match its format. It should be rebuilt with the script once you approve.
- **The environment check for rate settings (`MFG_*` variables).** That check is item 60 on the list.

## Files in `./out`

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `plant-context.md` | Draft plant profile (`## Plant context`). It records only the state of each rate, never a value |
| `config-profile-page.html` | Config profile page for the draft, marked DRAFT |
| `missing-data-list.html` | The 61 open questions, each with the skills it affects and how they're limited until answered, plus connector options |
| `export-request-spec.html` | Specs IT can use to set up exports for the six data sources that weren't in hand |

## What your three documents covered (all still unconfirmed)
- **`plant_overview.md`:** site, time zone, systems, shift times and the 23:30 MES export.
- **`equipment.csv`:** five assets, two cells and four work centers, used as the starting point for machine classes.
- **`rates_memo.txt`:** commercial rates, shown only in the internal section below. It also gave the scrap costing basis.

Everything taken from a file stays marked *inferred* until someone confirms it.

**Systems:** NetSuite, Microsoft 365 and Fusion are all exports or files for now. None of their connectors was available this session, and I didn't try to connect anything. Each connector's setup steps, quoted word for word from the plugin's table:
- **Oracle NetSuite:** "Enable the Oracle NetSuite connector in Claude's connector settings. Read and write; the sign-in picks your account, so there is no account ID to enter here"
- **Microsoft 365:** "Enable the Microsoft 365 connector in Claude's connector settings. Documents, mail and the export folder"
- **Autodesk Fusion:** "In the Fusion **desktop** app: *Preferences → General → API* → enable **Fusion MCP Server**. It runs locally on your machine and needs Fusion open with a document. If you changed the port from 27182, set `FUSION_MCP_PORT`"

**Time setup:** there's one row per data source (seven in total). Every timezone and timestamp format is unknown, and I couldn't compare clocks across systems because no event appears in two sources I have.

Shifts are 06:00–14:30 and 14:30–23:00, Monday to Friday, with Saturday overtime on request. **When your production day begins was not assumed. It's asked directly as item 26.**

Paused RFQs, supplier quotes and dashboard links will be kept on a private Open work page the first time you need one.

## Commercial rates — internal, check these before you say yes
*This is the only place these values appear. Once approved, they go on your private rates page, never the setup page, the config page or a customer quote.*

| Rate | Proposed value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Fully burdened shop rate | MILL-H 145, MILL-V 95, TURN 85, INSP 60 USD/h | rates_memo.txt (dated 1 Oct 2026) |

| Downtime cost per hour | not set | Not in the memo and never worked out from the shop rates |

## Missing-data list (full detail with impacts in `missing-data-list.html`)
- **A. Approval (1):** Approve the draft ("yes" or "yes, folder only") and give the name to record as approver.
- **B. Systems (2–6):**
  - Whether the NetSuite, Microsoft 365 and Fusion connectors will be turned on.
  - Maintenance lives in a spreadsheet: can it be exported nightly?
  - The MES's name.
- **C. NetSuite scope (7–15):**
  - Which record types exist, and which subsidiary, locations and items are this plant's.
  - Where the part revision is kept, which cost fields mean what (is standard costing on?), and where production work orders come from.
  - Which source wins when both an export and a connector have the data, and how long an RFQ can wait before it's stale (default 5 business days).
- **D. Exports (16–24):**
  - The exact export folder.
  - A sample MES production file and the window it covers.
  - A copy of `maintenance_log.csv`, and confirmation that `equipment.csv` is your full asset register.
  - Whether these exports exist: MES downtime, NetSuite, quality, planning, historian.
- **E. Time (25–30):**
  - Timezone and timestamp format for each source.
  - When the production day begins.
  - Which day late-running shifts and Saturday overtime count toward.
  - What counts as planned production time.
  - One event recorded in two systems, for the clock check.
  - What the 23:30 MES file covers.
- **F–G. Vocabulary and sites (31–33):** your terms for job, cell, lot and so on; summary-first or full-detail reports; is EPW1 your only site?
- **H. Capability (34–38):** material grades, in-house versus outside processes, the largest part each machine takes, demonstrated tolerances, certifications.
- **I. Machining data (39–45):**
  - Setup and tool-change times, each marked measured or estimated.
  - Cutting data or your Fusion tool library.
  - When to flag differing estimates (default 15%) and when cost data counts as too old.
  - The MILL-V work center has machines in both cells — confirm cells are assigned per machine.
  - Anodize lead time.
- **J. Standards and suppliers (46–49):** your certificate, supplier quality clauses, commercial terms, and approved suppliers by commodity.
- **K. Templates (50–54):** one real example each of your NCR, 8D, quote, supplier RFQ package and trade study.
- **L. Rates (55–61):**
  - Confirm how the work-center rates split into labor and burden.
  - Margin, including any customer or job-type exceptions.
  - How the material and outside-processing markups apply.
  - Downtime cost per hour.
  - Who is giving the rates, and whether the memo is still current.
  - Whether any `MFG_*` environment variables are set.
  - Confirm the scrap costing basis.

**Biggest impact if left open:**
- **Morning report:** OEE can't be calculated without the production-day start (26), planned production time (28), downtime data (20) and the plan export (23).
- **Quotes:** quote-build blocks its labor and margin lines until the rates are confirmed with a name (55, 56, 59).
- **Maintenance:** diagnosis has no maintenance history until `maintenance_log.csv` is provided (18).

**To finish setup:** say **"yes"** (installs the profile and creates your private setup and rates pages) or **"yes, folder only"**, and tell me who to record as approving it. Answers to any of the 61 questions can come in any order. Each one updates only its own line of the profile.
